nameStory: This plant gets its name "stringy stonecrop" from its trailing, string-like stems that spread across rocks and stone surfaces. Like other stonecrops, it's incredibly tough and can thrive in rocky, dry conditions where most plants would give up - truly living up to its ability to "crop" or grow from stones.
description: Stringy stonecrop is a low-growing, mat-forming succulent that spreads by trailing stems across the ground. This Asian native has thick, fleshy leaves arranged in groups of three and produces cheerful yellow star-shaped flowers in summer. The plant typically stays under 6 inches tall but can spread several feet wide, creating dense carpets of green foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, succulent leaves arranged in whorls of three around the stem, each leaf about fingernail-sized and smooth to the touch with a waxy feel

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals that bloom in flat-topped clusters, each flower about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading mats via long, trailing stems that root at nodes where they touch the ground, creating dense colonies

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Reddish to green trailing stems that feel firm and slightly rubbery, often rooting at joints where they contact soil

habitat: Look for stringy stonecrop in disturbed areas, old cemeteries, rock gardens, and stone walls where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in well-drained, sandy or rocky soils and tolerates poor, thin soils that would challenge most other plants. Often found growing alongside other tough plants in urban and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots from overwintered stems, with the succulent leaves becoming plump and vibrant.
seasonality.summer: Produces its characteristic bright yellow flowers from June through August, making identification easiest during this peak blooming period.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but the thick succulent leaves often take on reddish tinges, especially along the edges and stems.
seasonality.winter: Often stays partially evergreen in milder areas, with stems and leaves persisting under snow cover in a dormant state.

funFact: This tough little plant can survive being completely dried out for months - if you pull up a seemingly dead piece from a stone wall and give it water, it will often spring back to life like a botanical zombie!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other low-growing stonecrops, but stringy stonecrop is the only common one with leaves arranged consistently in groups of three. Remember: "three leaves free" for stringy stonecrop, while most others have opposite or scattered leaf arrangements.
contextualKnowledge: Though called "graveyard moss," this plant isn't actually a moss at all - it's a flowering succulent that just happens to grow well in the well-drained, undisturbed soil of old cemeteries. This common name confusion leads many people to overlook its pretty yellow flowers.
compareHints: Unlike biting stonecrop which has tiny needle-like leaves that taste peppery, stringy stonecrop has larger, flatter leaves in groups of three that are essentially tasteless. Woodland stonecrop is native and has white flowers, while stringy stonecrop is introduced with bright yellow blooms and much more aggressive spreading habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England stonecrops, biting stonecrop has the smallest, most tightly overlapping leaves and the most intense golden-yellow flowers.
Among New England's stonecrops, white stonecrop stands out for its pure white flowers and cylindrical leaves that look like tiny green hot dogs.
Tasteless stonecrop's six-spiral leaf arrangement sets it apart from most other stonecrops in New England.
Woodland stonecrop stands out from its stonecrop relatives by its preference for shade and its unique four-petaled white flowers – most other Sedum species have five yellow petals and love full sun.
Among New England's stonecrops, Spanish stonecrop is distinguished by its particularly dense, mat-forming growth and tendency toward reddish stem coloration.

Mexican Stonecrop stands out from other New England stonecrops by its bright yellow-green 'lemon coral' coloration, while Stringy Stonecrop is more blue-green and Biting Stonecrop has shorter, more tightly packed triangular leaves.

Unlike the common yellow-flowered biting stonecrop or the shade-loving woodland stonecrop with its distinctive three-leaf clusters, cliff stonecrop has pure white flowers and distinctly blue-green (glaucous) leaves.
Unlike the yellow-flowered biting stonecrop with its pointed, cone-shaped leaves, thick-leaved stonecrop has white or pink flowers and much plumper, rounder leaves.
Makino's stonecrop differs from Stringy Stonecrop by its more compact, less trailing growth habit and smaller stature.
